doc.title: Houston Person Part 2 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 2, 1998 [interview 2 of 2]

title: New album of ballads and the 78 rpm approach
summary: Person describes his upcoming album of standards that stresses melody, with short 4-5 minute tracks like 78s, and says the Parker, Dizzy and Miles solos were short yet complete.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Soon to be 76 you said. Tell me about your recent thing that’s coming out.

This is an album of standards, mostly ballads, and on it I’m stressing the melody, how strong the melodies are, with not too much emphasis on improvisation. But the improvisation is subtle. But I’m just stressing the melody and the strongness of songs from the great American songbook. Probably most of them you would consider, people would say have been over-done, but I wanted to do this set of songs, it really stressed a lot of content and melody.
When you say that it reminds me of something off this album that I’ll play a bit of when you did “As Time Goes By” that you treat that melody with so much care.
Oh yeah. I love the melody.
When you do that on this particular album does it make for shorter cuts? © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

That’s one thing about this is that I went back to the concept of doing it as if they were 78’s, so we went from anywhere from 4-5 minutes. There’s a track of “Laura” that is a little extended but the rest of them are in that time range. I’ve been trying to stress melody, keep simple, and not be too long.
Do you find that that’s something that you feel the jazz audience needs these days? To have a musician keep the songs perhaps a little shorter so that you don’t alienate anybody?

Well not necessarily. I think that if you don’t have anything to say for so long and trying to get it together on stage, I don’t go there. You should know what you’re going to say when you get up there and get it over with. So if you go back and listen to those 78’s, that Charlie Parker and Dizzy and Miles did, you’ll see that their solos were short and they did it all. I mean those things are amazing. And you try to play some of those solos, transcribe them, and you can’t. And they were the ones that were qualified to take long solos, and they didn’t.
